title: Afghanistan

cards.h: India's old friend and a new test
cards.b:
Afghanistan sits at the crossroads of South and Central Asia. For India it is a source of risk (terror groups, drugs) and an opportunity (a route to Central Asia, a friendly public, a counter to Pakistan's reach).

After the Taliban returned on 15 August 2021, India closed its embassy and watched. From 2022 it moved step by step to a pragmatic engagement. In October 2025 it upgraded its Kabul mission to an embassy. In 2026 the Pakistan–Taliban clashes added a new twist.

The examiner wants a balanced view: values versus interests, and engagement without recognition.

Between 2001 and 2021 India gave over $3 billion in aid, more than any other regional state. Major projects:

  • Zaranj–Delaram highway (218 km, 2009), a route linking to Iran's Chabahar.
  • Salma Dam (Afghan–India Friendship Dam, Herat, 2016).
  • Parliament building in Kabul (2015) and many schools, hospitals and training programmes.
  • Air Freight Corridor (2017) bypassing Pakistan.

The 2011 Strategic Partnership Agreement was Afghanistan's first such pact. India's line was 'Afghan-led, Afghan-owned, Afghan-controlled' peace. The book to know is Avinash Paliwal's My Enemy's Enemy: India in Afghanistan from the Soviet Invasion to the US Withdrawal (2017).

The 2020 Doha agreement between the US and the Taliban led to the US withdrawal in 2021. India's earlier ban on talking to the Taliban faded. Officials met Taliban leaders in Doha in 2021.

  • June 2022: a 'technical team' returned to the Kabul embassy to coordinate aid.
  • Aid: wheat, medicines, vaccines and earthquake relief, delivered through the UN and directly.
  • Visas and Afghan students: a limited regime; Afghan Sikhs and Hindus given priority.
  • January 2025: the Foreign Secretary met Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi in Dubai.
  • October 2025: India attended the 7th Moscow Format consultations (7 October 2025) and hosted Taliban Foreign Minister Muttaqi in Delhi. Jaishankar announced the upgrade of the Kabul technical mission to a full embassy.
  • January 2026: a Taliban-appointed chargé d'affaires took charge at the Afghan embassy in Delhi.

India has not formally recognised the Taliban. As of 2026 only Russia has (July 2025).

• Pakistan: relations between the Taliban and Pakistan have turned hostile over the TTP. Pakistan struck Afghan cities in February 2026 and declared 'open war' on 27 February; a ceasefire proved fragile and clashes continued through 2026. Islamabad accuses Kabul of being 'a colony of India'. India denies backing militants.
  • Terrorism: the Taliban condemned the Pahalgam attack (April 2025) and promised that Afghan soil will not be used against others.
  • Connectivity: access to Central Asia and Chabahar, minerals and markets.
  • China and Russia: both engage the Taliban. India does not want to leave the field.
  • People: Afghans' goodwill towards India remains high.

Pakistan's denial of land transit for trade stays a key hurdle. Air and sea routes are used instead.

• India has no land border with Afghanistan in practice. The Wakhan Corridor touches India's claimed territory in PoK, but Pakistan controls the access.
  • The Durand Line (1893) is the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. No Afghan government has accepted it. This is the root of the Pakistan–Taliban quarrel.
  • Pakistan's idea of 'strategic depth' in Afghanistan has clashed with Taliban nationalism.
  • Routes for India: Chabahar to Zaranj, then the Zaranj–Delaram highway; the INSTC; and the TAPI gas pipeline (Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India), which has been stalled for decades.

Afghanistan is also a mineral-rich country (copper, lithium, rare earths) and a corridor for Central Asian energy.

Pakistan

Helped create and shelter the Taliban, but now fights them over the TTP and the Durand Line.

China

Seeks mines, security for its Xinjiang border and a route for CPEC.

Russia and Iran

Talk to the Taliban, worried about ISKP. Russia recognised the Taliban in 2025.

Central Asian states

Want trade and security, and engage Kabul.

United States

Withdrew in 2021, but still wants counter-terror access and, according to Trump's 2025 remarks, Bagram.

India's position: not the biggest player, but a trusted one among ordinary Afghans.

• Women's rights: bans on girls' secondary education and women's work. India raises this in UN forums but ties are not conditional on it.
  • Terror groups: the UN lists several, including al-Qaeda, the Islamic State–Khorasan (ISKP) and Pakistan-focused groups like the TTP. India worries about LeT and JeM havens.
  • Chabahar: the US reimposed sanctions on the port in September 2025, granted a conditional waiver to 26 April 2026, and the position after that was still unclear. Check the latest status.
  • Recognition: a formal step would anger Western and domestic critics, and give Pakistan an argument.
  • Drugs and refugees.
  • US interest in Bagram: Trump said in 2025 he wanted it back.

A realist reading: states deal with whoever rules. India's influence in Kabul would vanish if it stayed away. A constructivist reading: India's identity as a democracy and its standing among Afghans (and its position on rights) set limits on how close it can go.

Paliwal argues India's policy has always been an anti-Pakistan hedge more than a love for any Afghan ruler. The Taliban-Pakistan rift in 2025–26 supports that view.

• Keeps the humanitarian channel strong: food, medicine, health teams.
  • Builds trade through air corridors and Iran.
  • Insists on an inclusive government and women's rights in statements.
  • Works with Russia, Iran and Central Asia in the Moscow Format and the India–Central Asia Dialogue (2019).
  • Wants a written guarantee against terrorism from Afghan soil.

Present tense for the exam: India engages but does not recognise. It has upgraded to an embassy and accepted a Taliban diplomat, which is 'recognition in all but name' to some critics.

"India's Afghanistan policy after the Taliban takeover: continuity or change?" (typical)
"Evaluate the regional implications of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan for India." (typical)
"Why is Afghanistan important for India's connectivity to Central Asia?" (typical)

Structure: (1) history and Indian projects; (2) 2021 shock; (3) pragmatic engagement steps 2022–26; (4) drivers: Pakistan, terrorism, connectivity, Chinese and Russian presence; (5) limits: women's rights, recognition, sanctions; (6) way forward: engage on humanitarian and security, coordinate with regional states.
